{{Short description|1966 result in mathematical analysis}}
{{Distinguish|Carlson's theorem}}
'''Carleson's theorem''' is a fundamental result in [[mathematical analysis]] establishing the ([[Lebesgue measure|Lebesgue]]) [[Pointwise convergence#Almost everywhere convergence|pointwise almost everywhere convergence]] of [[Fourier series]] of [[Lp space|{{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>}} functions]], proved by [[Lennart Carleson]].<ref name="carleson">{{cite journal | last=Carleson | first=Lennart | authorlink=Lennart Carleson|title=On convergence and growth of partial sums of Fourier series | doi=10.1007/BF02392815 | mr=0199631 | year=1966 | journal=[[Acta Mathematica]] | volume=116 | issue=1 | pages=135–157| doi-access=free }}</ref> The name is also often used to refer to the extension of the result by [[Richard Hunt (mathematician)|Richard Hunt]] to {{math|''L''<sup>''p''</sup>}} functions for {{math|''p'' ∈ {{open-closed|1, ∞}}}} (also known as the ''Carleson&ndash;Hunt theorem'') and the analogous results for pointwise almost everywhere convergence of [[Fourier integral]]s, which can be shown to be equivalent by transference methods.<ref name="hunt">{{cite book | last=Hunt | first=Richard A. |authorlink=Richard Hunt (mathematician)| title=Orthogonal Expansions and their Continuous Analogues Proc. Conf., Edwardsville, Ill., 1967 | publisher=Southern Illinois Univ. Press | location=Carbondale, Ill. | mr=0238019 | year=1968 | chapter=On the convergence of Fourier series | pages=235–255}}</ref>

==Statement of the theorem==
The result, as extended by Hunt, can be formally stated as follows:

{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = Let {{math|''f''}} be an {{math|''L''<sup>''p''</sup>}} [[periodic function]] for some {{math|''p'' &isin; {{open-closed|1, ∞}}}}, with [[Fourier coefficients]] <math>\hat{f}(n)</math>.  Then <math display="block">\lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{|n| \leq N} \hat{f}(n) e^{inx} = f(x)</math> for [[almost every]]&nbsp;{{mvar|x}}.}}

The analogous result for Fourier integrals is:

{{block indent | em = 1.5 | text = Let {{math|''f'' &isin; ''L''<sup>''p''</sup>('''R''')}} for some {{math|''p'' &isin; {{open-closed|1, 2}}}} have [[Fourier transform]] <math>\hat{f}(\xi)</math>.  Then <math display="block">\lim_{R \to \infty} \int_{|\xi| \leq R} \hat{f}(\xi) e^{2 \pi i x \xi} \, d\xi = f(x)</math> for almost every {{math|''x'' &isin; '''R'''}}.}}

==History==
A fundamental question about Fourier series, asked by [[Joseph Fourier|Fourier]] himself at the beginning of the 19th century, is whether the Fourier series of a [[continuous function|continuous]] function [[pointwise convergence|converges pointwise]] to the function.

By strengthening the continuity assumption slightly one can easily show that the Fourier series converges everywhere. For example, if a function has [[bounded variation]] then its Fourier series converges everywhere to the local average of the function. In particular, if a function is [[continuously differentiable]] then its Fourier series converges to it everywhere. This was proven by [[Dirichlet]], who expressed his belief that he would soon be able to extend his result to cover all continuous functions. Another way to obtain convergence everywhere is to change the summation method. For example, [[Fejér's theorem]] shows that if one replaces ordinary summation by [[Cesàro summation]] then the Fourier series of any continuous function [[converges uniformly]] to the function. Further, it is easy to show that the Fourier series of any {{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>}} function converges to it in {{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>}} norm.

After Dirichlet's result, several experts, including Dirichlet, [[Riemann]], [[Weierstrass]] and [[Dedekind]], stated their belief  that the Fourier series of any continuous function would converge everywhere. This was disproved by [[Paul du Bois-Reymond]], who showed in 1876 that there is  [[Uniform boundedness theorem#Example: pointwise convergence of Fourier series|a continuous function whose Fourier series diverges at one point]].

The almost-everywhere convergence of Fourier series for {{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>}} functions was postulated by [[Nikolai Nikolaevich Luzin|N. N. Luzin]],<ref name="luzin">{{citation|first=N.N.|last=Luzin|title=The integral and trigonometric series (In Russian)|place=Moscow-Leningrad|year=1915}} (Thesis; also: Collected Works, Vol. 1, Moscow, 1953, pp.&nbsp;48–212)</ref> and the problem was known as ''Luzin's conjecture'' up until its proof by Carleson.<ref name="carleson"/> {{harvtxt|Kolmogorov|1923}} showed that the analogue of Luzin's conjecture for {{math|''L''<sup>1</sup>}} is false by finding such a function whose Fourier series diverges almost everywhere (improved slightly in 1926 to diverging everywhere).<ref name="kolmogorov">{{cite journal | last1=Kolmogorov | first1=Andrey Nikolaevich | author1-link=Andrey Nikolaevich Kolmogorov | title= Une série de Fourier–Lebesgue divergente presque partout | url=https://eudml.org/doc/213617 | year=1923 | journal=Fundamenta Mathematicae | volume=4 | pages= 324–328| doi=10.4064/fm-4-1-324-328 | doi-access=free }}</ref> Before Carleson's result, the best known estimate for the [[partial sums]] {{math|''s''<sub>''n''</sub>}} of the Fourier series of a function in {{math|''L''<sup>''p''</sup>}} was
<math display="block">s_n(x) = o(\log (n)^{1/p})\text{ almost everywhere}.</math>
In other words, the function {{math|''s<sub>n</sub>''(''x'')}} can still grow to infinity at any given point ''x'' as one takes more and more terms of the Fourier series into account, though the growth must be quite slow (slower than the [[logarithm]] of {{mvar|n}} to a small power). This result was
proved by Kolmogorov–Seliverstov–Plessner for {{math|1=''p'' = 2}}, by [[G. H. Hardy]] for {{math|1=''p'' = 1}}, and by Littlewood–Paley for {{math|''p'' > 1}}.<ref name="zygmund">{{cite book | last1=Zygmund | first1=A. |author-link=Antoni Zygmund | title=Trigonometric Series. Vol. I, II | orig-year=1935 | title-link=Trigonometric Series | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | edition=3rd | series=Cambridge Mathematical Library | isbn=978-0-521-89053-3 | mr=1963498 | year=2002}}</ref> This result had not been improved for several decades, leading some experts to suspect that it was the best possible and that Luzin's conjecture was false. Kolmogorov's [[counterexample]] in {{math|''L''<sup>1</sup>}} was unbounded in any [[interval (mathematics)|interval]], but it was thought to be only a matter of time before a continuous counterexample was found. Carleson said in a 2007 interview that he started by trying to find a continuous counterexample and at one point thought he had a method that would construct one, but realized eventually that his approach could not work. He then tried instead to prove Luzin's conjecture since the failure of his counterexample convinced him that it was probably true.<ref name="raussen-skau">{{cite journal | last1=Raussen | first1=Martin | last2=Skau | first2=Christian | title=Interview with Abel Prize recipient Lennart Carleson | url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200702/comm-carleson.pdf  | mr=2285126 | year=2007 | journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] | volume=54 | issue=2 | pages=223–229}}</ref>

Carleson's original proof is exceptionally hard to read, and although several authors have simplified the argument there are still no easy proofs of his theorem. Expositions of the original paper include {{harvtxt|Kahane|1995}},<ref name="kahane">{{cite book | last1=Kahane | first1=Jean-Pierre | author1-link=Jean-Pierre Kahane | title=Séminaire Bourbaki | publisher=[[Société Mathématique de France]] | location=Paris | mr=1610981 | year=1995 | volume=9 | chapter=Sommes partielles des séries de Fourier (d'après L. Carleson) | chapter-url=http://www.numdam.org/item?id=SB_1964-1966__9__491_0 | pages=491–507}}</ref> {{harvtxt|Mozzochi|1971}},<ref name="mozzochi">{{cite book | last1=Mozzochi | first1=Charles J. | title=On the pointwise convergence of Fourier series | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | location=Berlin, New York | series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics, Vol. 199 | doi=10.1007/BFb0061167 | mr=0445205 | year=1971 | volume=199| isbn=978-3-540-05475-7 }}</ref> {{harvtxt|Jørsboe|Mejlbro|1982}},<ref name="jorsboe-mejlbro">{{cite book | last1=Jørsboe | first1=Ole G. | last2=Mejlbro | first2=Leif | title=The Carleson-Hunt theorem on Fourier series | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | location=Berlin, New York | series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics | isbn=978-3-540-11198-6 | doi=10.1007/BFb0094072 | mr=653477 | year=1982 | volume=911}}</ref> and {{harvtxt|Arias de Reyna|2002}}.<ref>{{cite book| last=Arias de Reyna | first=Juan | title=Pointwise convergence of Fourier series | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | location=Berlin, New York | series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics | isbn=978-3-540-43270-8 | doi=10.1007/b83346 | mr=1906800 | year=2002 | volume=1785}}</ref> [[Charles Fefferman]] published a new proof of Hunt's extension which proceeded by bounding a [[maximal operator]].<ref name="fefferman">{{cite journal | doi=10.2307/1970917 | last1=Fefferman | first1=Charles | author1-link=Charles Fefferman | title=Pointwise convergence of Fourier series | mr=0340926 | year=1973 | journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |series=Second Series | volume=98 | pages=551–571 | issue=3| jstor=1970917 }}</ref> This, in turn, inspired a much simplified proof of the ''L''<sup>2</sup> result by {{harvs|txt|first1=Michael |last1=Lacey|author1-link=Michael Lacey (mathematician)|first2=Christoph|last2= Thiele|year=2000}},<ref name="lacey-thiele">{{cite journal|last1=Lacey |first1=Michael |last2=Thiele |first2=Christoph |title=A proof of boundedness of the Carleson operator |mr=1783613 |year=2000 |journal=Mathematical Research Letters |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=361–370 |doi=10.4310/mrl.2000.v7.n4.a1 |doi-access=free }}</ref> explained in more detail in {{harvtxt|Lacey|2004}}.<ref name="lacey04">{{cite journal | last1=Lacey | first1=Michael T. | title=Carleson's theorem: proof, complements, variations | arxiv=math/0307008 | mr=2091007 | year=2004 | journal=Publicacions Matemàtiques | volume=48 | issue=2 | pages=251–307 | doi=10.5565/publmat_48204_01| s2cid=16121272 }}</ref> The books {{harvtxt|Fremlin|2003}} and {{harvtxt|Grafakos|2014}} also give proofs of Carleson's theorem.<ref name="fremlin">{{cite book | last1=Fremlin | first1=David H. | title=Measure theory | url=http://www.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/mt.htm | publisher=Torres Fremlin, Colchester | isbn=978-0-9538129-2-9 | mr=2462280 | year=2003 | volume=2 | access-date=2010-09-09 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101101220236/http://www.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/mt.htm# | archive-date=2010-11-01 | url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="grafakos">{{cite book | last1=Grafakos | first1=Loukas | title=Modern Fourier analysis | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | location=New York | edition=Third | series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics | isbn=978-1-4939-1229-2 | doi=10.1007/978-1-4939-1230-8 | mr=3243741 | year=2014 | volume=250}}</ref> The theorem was formalized in [[Lean 4]] in 2025.

{{harvtxt|Katznelson|1966}} showed that for any set of [[measure zero]] there is a continuous periodic function whose Fourier series diverges at all points of the set (and possibly elsewhere).<ref name="katznelson">{{cite journal | last1=Katznelson | first1=Yitzhak | title=Sur les ensembles de divergence des séries trigonométriques | url=http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/tresc.php?wyd=2&tom=26 | mr=0199632 | year=1966 | journal= Studia Mathematica | volume=26 | issue=3 | pages=301–304| doi=10.4064/sm-26-3-305-306 | doi-access=free }}</ref> When combined with Carleson's theorem this shows that there is a continuous function whose Fourier series diverges at all points of a given set of [[real number|reals]] if and only if the set has measure zero.

The extension of Carleson's theorem to {{math|''L''<sup>''p''</sup>}} for {{math|''p'' > 1}} was stated to be a "rather obvious" extension of the case {{math|1=''p'' = 2}} in Carleson's paper, and was proved by Hunt.<ref name="hunt"/> Carleson's result was improved further by {{harvtxt|Sjölin|1971}} to the space {{math|''L''&thinsp;log<sub>+</sub>(''L'')log<sub>+</sub>log<sub>+</sub>(''L'')}}<ref name="sjolin">{{cite journal | last1=Sjölin | first1=Per | title=Convergence almost everywhere of certain singular integrals and multiple Fourier series | doi=10.1007/BF02383638 | mr=0336222 | year=1971 | journal=Arkiv för Matematik  | volume=9 | issue=1–2 | pages=65–90| bibcode=1971ArM.....9...65S | doi-access=free }}</ref> and by {{harvtxt|Antonov|1996}} to the space {{math|''L''&thinsp;log<sub>+</sub>(''L'')log<sub>+</sub>log<sub>+</sub>log<sub>+</sub>(''L'')}}.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Antonov|first=N. Yu.|mr=1407066|year=1996| journal=East Journal on Approximations | volume=2 | issue=2 | title=Convergence of Fourier series | pages=187–196}}</ref> (Here {{math|log<sub>+</sub>(''L'')}} is {{math|log(''L'')}} if {{math|''L'' > 1}} and {{math|0}} otherwise, and if {{math|''φ''}} is a function then {{math|''φ''(''L'')}} stands for the space of functions {{math|''f''}} such that {{math|''φ''({{abs|''f''(''x'')}})}} is [[integrable function|integrable]].)

{{harvtxt|Konyagin|2000}} improved Kolmogorov's counterexample by finding functions with everywhere-divergent Fourier series in a space slightly larger than {{math|''L''&thinsp;log<sub>+</sub>(''L'')<sup>1/2</sup>}}.<ref name="konyagin">{{cite journal | last1=Konyagin | first1=S. V. | title=On the divergence everywhere of trigonometric Fourier series | mr=1753494 | year=2000 | journal=Rossiĭskaya Akademiya Nauk. Matematicheskii Sbornik | volume=191 | issue=1 | pages=103–126 | doi=10.1070/sm2000v191n01abeh000449| bibcode=2000SbMat.191...97K | s2cid=250745433 }}</ref> One can ask if there is in some sense a largest natural space of functions whose Fourier series converge almost everywhere. The simplest candidate for such a space that is consistent with the results of Antonov and Konyagin is {{math|''L''&thinsp;log<sub>+</sub>(''L'')}}.

The extension of Carleson's theorem to Fourier series and integrals in several variables is made more complicated as there are many different ways in which one can sum the coefficients; for example, one can sum over increasing balls, or increasing rectangles.  Convergence of rectangular partial sums (and indeed general polygonal partial sums) follows from the one-dimensional case, but the spherical summation problem is still [[open problem|open]] for {{math|''L''<sup>2</sup>}}.

==The Carleson operator==
The Carleson operator {{math|''C''}} is the non-linear operator defined by
<math display="block"> Cf(x) = \sup_N\left|\int_{-N}^N \hat f(y)e^{2\pi i xy} \, dy\right|</math>

It is relatively easy to show that the Carleson–Hunt theorem follows from the [[bounded operator|boundedness]] of the Carleson operator from {{math|''L''<sup>''p''</sup>('''R''')}} to itself  for {{math|1 < ''p'' < ∞}}. However, proving that it is bounded is difficult, and this was actually what Carleson proved.
